source_text: Sed quod promisce obseruatur per ecclesias quasi incertum, id retractandum est, uelarine debeant uirgines, an non. qui enim uirginibus indulgent capitis immunitatem, hoc niti uidentur, quod apostolus non uirgines nominatim, sed mulieres designauerit uelandas esse, nec sexum, ut diceret feminas, sed gradum sexus, dicendo mulieres. nam si sexum nominasset, feminas dicendo, absolute definisset de omni muliere, at cum unum gradum sexus nominat, alium tacendo secernit. potuit enim, inquiunt, aut et uirgines nominare specialiter aut compendio generaliter feminas.
thought_title: Should virgins be veiled? The opponents' argument from Paul's wording
orientation: Tertullian is opening the debate over whether virgins must be veiled, and here he states the argument of those who allow virgins to go with uncovered heads.
pass_a_gloss: But what is observed indiscriminately through the churches as if uncertain, this must be reconsidered: whether virgins ought to be veiled or not. For those who grant virgins exemption of the head seem to rely on this, that the apostle designated not virgins by name, but women, as the ones who must be veiled, and that he designated not the sex, so as to say females, but a degree of the sex, by saying women. For if he had named the sex, by saying females, he would have defined absolutely concerning every woman, but when he names one degree of the sex, he separates the other by being silent. For he could, they say, either name virgins specifically, or, by way of summary, females generally.

choices.why: Keeps the legal force of immunitas as a release from the obligation to cover the head, matching the debate's terms.
Gradus is a rank or stage within the category of sex; 'degree' preserves the technical distinction Tertullian is attacking.
Compendium means a short cut or abridgment; the opponents mean Paul could have used the general term females as a brief way of covering all.
Marks the opponents' voice, as the brief indicates, without adding a noun.

pass_b_english: But since the churches observe this practice without distinction, as if the matter were uncertain, it must be reconsidered: should virgins be veiled or not? Those who allow virgins to go with uncovered heads seem to rely on this argument: the apostle did not name virgins specifically when he said women should be veiled. They argue that he did not name the sex itself by saying females, but a degree of the sex by saying women. For if he had named the sex, saying females, he would have made an absolute ruling about every woman. But when he names one degree of the sex, he separates another by remaining silent. He could have, they say, either named virgins specifically or, by way of summary, females generally.

polish.changed: Clarified that the argument belongs to the opponents, made the sentence order more natural, and smoothed the phrasing for reading aloud while preserving every claim and qualification.
